standards.title: Customer service is the heart of WNF
standards.why: Our edge is the relationship we build with every customer who walks through the door. The work that defines WNF is on the floor — meeting customers, answering real questions, sharing what we know and what we love about products. Everything else supports that.
standards.how: However your shift starts, ask yourself: who's in the store right now, and how can I make their visit better? That's the job.

standards.title: Two ways to be great at customer service
standards.why: Excellence on our floor takes two forms, and we value both. (1) KNOWLEDGE — deep curiosity about natural foods, sourcing, and health. Willing to have real conversations with customers about what they're working through. (2) PASSION — genuine excitement about a great new chocolate bar, the year's best oregano, a product you love. The kind of enthusiasm customers feel from across the room.
standards.how: Lean into whichever archetype fits you. Knowledge takes time and study — partner with senior staff and ask questions. Passion shows up when you find products that genuinely move you — let that come through when you talk to customers.

standards.title: We hold a high bar — together
standards.why: WNF's standards are deliberately high. The team holds them collectively, not because of pressure, but because we're proud of what we're building. When standards are clear and consistent, everyone knows what to expect of each other and the team gets stronger.
standards.how: Know what the standard looks like. Ask if you're not sure. If something's slipping — including your own work — the team helps each other recalibrate. Honest conversations are how the standard holds.

standards.title: Anchors lead, everyone covers
standards.why: Roles describe primary responsibility, not exclusive ownership. If a wellness item is missing from the shelf and you spot it, the answer isn't 'that's BoH's job' — it's grab one and put it out. The store works because the team covers each other's small fires.
standards.how: Know what you anchor. But also: if you see a problem that takes thirty seconds to fix, fix it. Don't wait for the named owner. Don't pass it along.

standards.title: Sam and Tyler speak for Joshua
standards.why: When Joshua isn't in the building — and especially in critical moments, edge cases, or anything unknown — Sam (Culture Queen / Comms Lead) and Tyler (Deputy) carry Joshua's authority. Their word is Joshua's word. This is how the standard holds when the room changes. No going around them, no waiting it out, no second-guessing.
standards.how: If Joshua isn't reachable and a call needs to be made, route to Sam or Tyler. Sam carries culture, comms, and crew direction; Tyler carries BoH, receiving, and FoH-deputy calls. Their decision stands. Joshua backs them, every time.

standards.title: Communication — escalation tiers
standards.why: Our team is building cleaner habits around what's urgent vs. what can wait. Most things don't need to interrupt a manager or Joshua immediately — but the ones that do, should. Knowing the difference is part of the job.
standards.how: Use the urgency triage cards below to calibrate. When in doubt, ask your shift lead or manager. The Ops Assistant supports the team on getting communication routed cleanly.

standards.title: Joshua's working hours — when to bring what
standards.why: Joshua's day has rhythms. 5am–12pm is the office / strategic block — best for written briefs, decisions, and bigger questions. 1pm–5pm is floor presence at WNF ('in the pit') — bring floor-level questions and customer-facing items. 5pm–9pm is wrap-up time — good for follow-ups and end-of-day asks. Mon–Thu lean WNF; Fri–Sun lean portfolio.
standards.how: Match the question to the block. Strategic asks → morning brief or async. Floor questions → afternoon in the pit. End-of-day catch-ups → 5–9pm. Save the morning for the things that actually need real thought.

triage.label: Call or text right away
items: Customer issue that no one on the floor can resolve
Something on fire — POS down, cooler down, plumbing leak, power outage
Anything truly critical or costly that needs to move fast

items: Staff situation a manager wants Joshua looped in on
Property issue trending toward bigger (slow leak, intermittent HVAC)

triage.label: Email — Joshua reviews in the morning block
items: FYI for Joshua or for a teammate who's off shift
Ideas, suggestions, or proposals that need real thought

triage.label: Handle in seat — no need to escalate
items: Routine supply restocks within established parameters
Day-to-day decisions inside your role's authority
Standard commodity supplies (post-its, paper, etc.) — your role can solve it

rules.title: 5am–12pm = strategy window
rules.body: This is when written briefs, decisions, big asks, and creative work belong. The ops assistant should funnel anything requiring real thought into this window.

rules.title: 1pm–5pm = 'in the pit' at WNF
rules.body: Joshua is on the floor at WNF, fully reactive, customer-facing. People pull him left and right. Don't try to talk strategy with him during this window — he'll be in floor-mode, not decision-mode. This is when he's most accessible to staff and customers physically, least accessible mentally for new ideas.

rules.title: 5pm–9pm = clean-up / wrap-up window
rules.body: Loose ends, follow-ups, the day's tail. Better than the pit window for low-friction asks, end-of-day briefs, and items that need acknowledgment but not deep thought. Don't save high-stakes decisions for here — those go in the morning block.

rules.title: Reachable, with cleaner signal
rules.body: Joshua keeps his phone open. The team is building cleaner habits around what's urgent vs. what can wait. The Ops Assistant supports this — bring questions, get coached on routing.

rules.title: INVERT runs seasonally
rules.body: Spring (turnovers, post-move-out work) and deep winter (cold weather repairs) are the busy windows on the property side. Summer and fall are quieter — good time to plan ahead and build systems.
